texts.0: SP, due to a late and insufficient power reduction as the closure was being killed, did not stabilize airspeed in route position within the published tolerance. Airspeed diverged more than 15 knots from the route airspeed and the aircraft continued forward of the briefed position with the overtake unarrested. The IP had to take the throttle and reset the airspeed before the position could be re-established.
texts.1: SP, due to a throttle input made in one large step rather than in anticipation of the closure rate, did not control airspeed in route position as required. The deviation reached the 15 knot limit and persisted while the aircraft drifted forward, and it was reduced only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP. The correction was delayed but the aircraft remained inside the limit.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late power reduction at the start of the stabilization, did not hold the route airspeed within the tight tolerance. Airspeed opened between 5 and 15 knots from the briefed value with a visible overtake building. SP recognized the trend on his own, reduced power and re-established the route airspeed without any prompting or intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled airspeed in route position accurately, keeping the deviation within 5 knots of the briefed route airspeed throughout the rejoin. Power was applied in anticipation of the closure rate, so the overtake was killed at the correct point without oscillation. Corrections were small, prompt and made before the deviation could develop.
texts.4: SP flew the airspeed in route position with negligible deviation, holding the briefed value with only a couple of knots of variation from initial closure to stabilization. Power handling was continuous and anticipatory, so no correction was ever required after the position was reached. The airspeed control was of an exceptional standard for this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed in route position inside the standards, but the deviation stayed consistently on the fast side and every correction was made after the overtake had become visible rather than in anticipation of it. The trend was toward a late kill of the closure, which will not be tolerated as rejoin airspeeds increase. SP is expected to anticipate the power reduction and re-center the airspeed control on the briefed route value in subsequent sorties.

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch input applied while attention was fixed on the closure rather than on the vertical position, did not maintain altitude relative to No1 level within the published tolerance. The vertical displacement exceeded 100 feet from lead level and continued to increase during the final portion of the rejoin. The IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the aircraft on the lead level before the route position could be assumed.
texts.1: SP, due to an uncorrected pitch trim condition carried into the rejoin, did not hold the aircraft on No1 level as required. The vertical displacement reached the 100 foot limit and was allowed to remain there while the closure continued, and it was corrected only after direct verbal instruction from the IP. The recovery to lead level was late but no control intervention was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to a small pitch excursion during the power change, did not hold the aircraft precisely on No1 level. The vertical displacement opened to between 50 and 100 feet from lead level during the closure phase. SP detected the split against the lead aircraft, applied a smooth pitch correction and re-established the lead level in good time and without prompting.
texts.3: SP maintained the aircraft on No1 level accurately, keeping the vertical displacement within 50 feet of lead level throughout the closure and into the route position. Pitch corrections were small and made against the visual reference of the lead aircraft rather than against the instruments. The vertical position was stable at the moment the route position was assumed.
texts.4: SP flew the rejoin essentially on the lead level, with a vertical displacement that never became apparent against the lead aircraft reference and remained far inside the tolerance. Pitch was controlled continuously so that no discrete correction was required at any point of the closure. The result was an exceptionally stable vertical geometry throughout the maneuver.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft within the vertical standards relative to No1 level, but a repeated tendency to fly slightly high during the closure required a correction on each rejoin. The vertical position was acceptable yet it was reactive rather than maintained, and at higher closure rates this pattern will produce a displacement outside the limit. SP is expected to reference lead level continuously and eliminate the high tendency in the following sorties.

error_modes.label: Smooth and solid aircraft control during the rejoin

texts.0: SP, due to control inputs made in reaction to the changing sight picture instead of being flown in anticipation of it, did not control the aircraft in a smooth and solid manner. Roll and pitch inputs were abrupt and produced a divergent oscillation in the closure geometry that continued to grow. The IP took control to stabilize the aircraft and complete the rejoin.
texts.1: SP, due to an over-controlled response on the roll axis while attempting to hold the rejoin line, did not fly the aircraft smoothly and solidly. Inputs were coarse and were followed immediately by opposite inputs, so the aircraft oscillated about the intended flight path until the IP verbally directed a relaxation of the inputs. The technique improved only after that prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a stiff grip on the stick during the first part of the closure, did not fly the aircraft with the required smoothness. Control inputs were slightly abrupt and produced small, visible corrections in the geometry. SP recognized the over-control, relaxed the inputs and flew the remainder of the rejoin smoothly and solidly without prompting.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth and solid manner throughout the rejoin, applying continuous small inputs rather than discrete corrections. The flight path stayed steady through the closure and the stabilization in route position was accomplished without any oscillation. Aircraft handling was accurate and consistent with the criteria.
texts.4: SP flew the aircraft with exceptional smoothness and solidity, with control inputs so well anticipated that the closure appeared to develop without correction. Roll, pitch and power were coordinated continuously and the aircraft settled into route position in one motion. The handling standard was well above what is expected at this point of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP flew the rejoin within standards, but control inputs remained slightly abrupt on the roll axis and each correction was larger than the deviation demanded. The aircraft remained solid overall, yet the tendency to over-control will degrade the geometry when closure rates increase. SP is expected to fly smaller, anticipatory inputs and demonstrate consistently smooth handling in the next formation sorties.

error_modes.label: Aspect angle and angle off awareness during closure

texts.0: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure and lateral separation, was not cognizant of Aspect Angle and Angle Off during the rejoin. The angle off was allowed to remain excessive well inside the point at which it had to be reduced, and the resulting geometry drove the aircraft toward an unsafe closure with No1. The IP took control to arrest the closure and reposition the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure and lateral separation, did not correctly assess Aspect Angle and Angle Off as the rejoin developed. The angle off was reduced only after the IP called the geometry, and by then the closure had reached the limit of what could be corrected by the SP alone. The rejoin was completed but the assessment of the geometry was consistently late.
texts.2: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure and lateral separation early in the maneuver, initially misread the Aspect Angle and carried more angle off than the rejoin required. The geometry opened toward the limit of an acceptable closure. SP reassessed the sight picture against No1, adjusted the angle off in good time and completed the rejoin without prompting or intervention.
texts.3: SP remained cognizant of Aspect Angle and Angle Off throughout the rejoin, reading the geometry accurately against the lead aircraft and adjusting the angle off progressively as the range closed. The closure was controlled by geometry rather than by power alone. The assessment of the sight picture was correct and timely at every stage.
texts.4: SP demonstrated an exceptional grasp of Aspect Angle and Angle Off, continuously trading angle off against range so that the closure decayed to zero exactly at the route position. No corrective adjustment of the geometry was required at any point of the rejoin. The situational picture of the formation geometry was of a standard well beyond this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP remained aware of Aspect Angle and Angle Off within standards, but the assessment of the geometry was made in discrete steps rather than continuously, and the angle off was reduced slightly later than the range warranted. The rejoin was safe, yet the tendency to read the sight picture late leaves little margin at higher closure rates. SP is expected to evaluate aspect and angle off continuously and to adjust the geometry earlier on subsequent rejoins.

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft position relative to No1 while attention moved inside the cockpit, did not continuously keep visual on the lead aircraft. Visual contact was lost during the closure and the aircraft continued to converge with the formation without a valid reference. The IP intervened, re-established the visual and directed the recovery from the rejoin geometry.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft position relative to No1, did not maintain a continuous visual on the lead aircraft during the rejoin. The scan was broken repeatedly for cockpit references and the lead was reacquired only after the IP called it, by which point the geometry had degraded to the edge of what was acceptable. Visual contact was regained but the lapse was corrected only on instruction.
texts.2: SP, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft position relative to No1 at the start of the maneuver, briefly interrupted the visual on the lead aircraft. The lead was momentarily lost against the background during the closure and the geometry began to open. SP re-acquired No1 quickly on his own initiative and maintained continuous visual for the remainder of the rejoin.
texts.3: SP continuously kept visual on No1 throughout the rejoin, holding the lead aircraft in the correct portion of the canopy from the initial closure to the route position. The visual scan was never broken for cockpit references during the critical closure phase. Visual contact was maintained exactly as the criteria require.
texts.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted and disciplined visual on No1 for the entire maneuver, keeping the lead aircraft in view while still monitoring the surrounding airspace. The visual reference was never in doubt at any point of the closure or the stabilization. The lookout discipline was exceptional for this stage of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP kept visual on No1 within standards, but the scan was drawn inside the cockpit more often than the maneuver required and the lead was briefly out of the primary field of view on two occasions. Visual contact was never actually lost, yet the pattern reduces the margin available if the lead maneuvers unexpectedly. SP is expected to keep the visual on No1 uninterrupted through the closure phase in subsequent sorties.

error_modes.label: Recognition of an unavoidable overshoot and timely call to the leader

texts.0: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in voicing a recognized unsafe condition, did not inform the formation leader that an overshoot had become unavoidable. The closure was pressed toward the route position with no call made and no overshoot initiated, and the aircraft arrived with an unsafe overtake on No1. The IP made the call and took control to execute the overshoot.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in voicing a recognized unsafe condition, did not inform the formation leader of the developing overshoot in a timely manner. The call was made only after the IP directed it, by which time the closure had reached the limit at which the overshoot could still be flown safely. The overshoot was subsequently executed but the notification was late.
texts.2: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in voicing a recognized unsafe condition at the first indication of excess closure, delayed the call to the formation leader. The overtake had already become apparent before the transmission was made. SP then informed the leader on his own initiative, in good time to execute the overshoot safely and without any intervention.
texts.3: SP recognized that the overshoot was unavoidable and informed the formation leader promptly and clearly, then executed the overshoot safely as briefed. The call was made early enough for the leader to account for it, and the flight path selected kept the required separation from No1 at all times. The handling of the situation met the criteria in full.
texts.4: SP identified the developing overshoot at the earliest point at which it was detectable, passed a concise and unambiguous call to the formation leader and flew a controlled overshoot with generous separation from No1. The decision, the communication and the execution were made without hesitation and with no degradation of the formation. The airmanship demonstrated was exceptional at this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP informed the formation leader of the overshoot within acceptable time and flew it safely, but the recognition of the excess closure came late and the call was made only once the overtake was clearly established. The outcome was within standards, yet the reluctance to transmit at the first indication leaves little time for the leader to react. SP is expected to call an unavoidable overshoot at the point of recognition rather than at the point of certainty.

error_modes.label: Break out on loss of visual during overshoot

texts.0: SP, due to an attempt to search for the lead aircraft while continuing the overshoot flight path, did not execute a timely Break Out after visual contact with the formation leader was lost. The aircraft remained in the formation airspace without a visual reference and the separation from No1 was unknown. The IP took control, executed the Break Out and re-established safe separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed decision after visual contact with No1 was lost during the overshoot, did not initiate the Break Out on his own initiative. The aircraft was held on the existing flight path until the IP directed the maneuver, and by that point the separation had reduced to the minimum acceptable. The Break Out was then flown correctly but entirely on instruction.
texts.2: SP, due to a short delay in accepting that the lead aircraft could not be reacquired, did not initiate the Break Out at the earliest opportunity during the overshoot. A brief further search was made before the decision was taken. SP then executed the Break Out on his own initiative, in good time and with the correct direction and control inputs, requiring no intervention.
texts.3: SP lost visual contact with No1 during the overshoot and executed a timely Break Out on his own initiative, turning away from the last known position of the lead aircraft with a positive and controlled input. Separation was established quickly and the situation was reported to the leader. The response met the criteria without qualification.
texts.4: SP responded to the loss of visual contact during the overshoot with an immediate, decisive Break Out flown in the correct direction, achieving separation with no delay whatsoever and passing a clear call to the formation leader. The decision was taken without any attempt to press the search for No1. The discipline and decisiveness shown were exceptional for this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP executed the Break Out after losing visual on No1 within acceptable limits, but the decision was preceded by a period of continued searching and the initial turn away was less positive than the situation demanded. Separation was achieved, yet the delay consumed margin that should be preserved for exactly this case. SP is expected to treat loss of visual contact as an immediate trigger for Break Out on subsequent sorties.

error_modes.label: Straight ahead tactical rejoin per Techniques and Procedures Manual

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect recollection of the required tactical spacing and stabilization point, did not execute the straight ahead tactical rejoin according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The aircraft was flown to a position and a lateral spacing other than the one specified for a tactical rejoin, and the closure was not stabilized at the prescribed point. The IP intervened to reposition the aircraft and complete the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to an incorrect recollection of the sequence prescribed for the tactical rejoin, did not execute the maneuver in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual. The lateral spacing and the stabilization point were established only after the IP described the required position, and the profile was flown correctly only from that point onward. The end result was acceptable but the procedure was recalled and applied late.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation over the prescribed spacing for the tactical rejoin, did not initially fly the maneuver exactly as published. The aircraft was established slightly outside the intended tactical position during the closure. SP recognized the discrepancy against the briefed picture, corrected the spacing in good time and completed the tactical rejoin as prescribed without prompting or intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the straight ahead tactical rejoin in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, establishing the correct lateral spacing and stabilizing the closure at the prescribed point. The sequence was flown from memory in the correct order and without hesitation. The maneuver met the published procedure in full.
texts.4: SP flew the straight ahead tactical rejoin exactly as published, with the tactical spacing established precisely and the closure decaying to zero at the prescribed position without any adjustment. The sequence was executed with full spare capacity, which allowed the lookout and the formation picture to be maintained throughout. The standard achieved on the tactical rejoin was exceptional for this point of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP executed the straight ahead tactical rejoin within the published procedure, but the spacing was established by successive adjustments rather than being flown to directly, and the stabilization point was reached slightly late. The maneuver was correct in substance, yet the sequence still consumes more capacity than it should. SP is expected to fly the tactical rejoin to the prescribed spacing in one continuous profile in the sorties that follow.

error_modes.label: Stabilization and holding of the route position after the rejoin

texts.0: SP, due to a failure to kill the residual closure before arriving abeam No1, did not stabilize the aircraft in the route position. The aircraft moved fore and aft along the wing line with no fixed reference established and the lateral spacing continued to change after the rejoin was nominally complete. The IP took control to stabilize the aircraft in the route position.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on power changes alone rather than on a stable visual reference, did not stabilize the aircraft in route position as required. The aircraft continued to move relative to No1 at the limit of the acceptable position and was settled only after the IP described the reference to be used. The position was eventually held but only after direct instruction.
texts.2: SP, due to a small residual closure carried into the arrival, did not settle immediately into the route position. The aircraft drifted forward of the intended position before the reference was established. SP identified the drift against the lead aircraft, applied a small power reduction and stabilized the route position in good time without prompting.
texts.3: SP stabilized the aircraft in the route position accurately at the completion of the rejoin, killing the closure at the correct point and establishing a fixed visual reference on No1. The position was then held steadily with small anticipatory power and control inputs. The arrival and the stabilization met the required standard.
texts.4: SP arrived in the route position with the closure decayed exactly to zero and held the position with no perceptible movement relative to No1 for the remainder of the maneuver. The reference was established immediately and the position was maintained with minimal, continuous inputs. The precision of the arrival and the station keeping was exceptional at this stage.
texts.marginal: SP stabilized the aircraft in the route position within standards, but the arrival required two power corrections before the position settled and the aircraft continued to move slowly relative to No1 thereafter. The position was acceptable, yet it was maintained by correction rather than by a stable reference. SP is expected to kill the closure at the correct point and hold a steady reference on No1 from the moment the route position is reached.

error_modes.label: Generation of the initial 20 to 30 knot overtake

texts.0: SP, due to a power application that did not build the initial 20 to 30 knot overtake called for on a straight ahead rejoin, did not generate a usable closure on No1. The overtake was set more than 15 knots away from the briefed band, so the rejoin either stagnated with no range reduction or the aircraft ran in with closure that could no longer be killed. The IP had to take the throttle and reset the overtake before the rejoin could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to a hesitant throttle movement after the rejoin signal, did not establish the initial overtake as briefed. The airspeed differential sat at the 15 knot edge of the acceptable band and stayed there while the range hardly changed, and the correction came only after the IP called for the power. The rejoin remained inside limits but was flown on IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the closure actually being produced, did not establish the 20 to 30 knot overtake at the start of the rejoin. The airspeed differential was between 5 and 15 knots off the briefed band and the initial range reduction was slower than planned. SP compared the closure against the sight picture, corrected the power on his own and completed the rejoin within the standards.
texts.3: SP generated the initial overtake correctly, setting an airspeed differential inside 5 knots of the briefed 20 to 30 knot band immediately after the rejoin signal. The closure was established at once and produced a steady range reduction toward the bid point. Power handling matched the technique of the manual without further adjustment.
texts.4: SP established the initial overtake with negligible error, placing the airspeed differential within the briefed band in one smooth power application. The closure was correct from the first seconds and needed no revision at any point of the run in. The energy management on the rejoin was of an exceptional standard for this stage.
texts.marginal: SP produced an initial overtake inside the standards, but it was consistently set at the low end of the band and only after a delay, so the rejoin was slow to develop each time. The closure was legal yet always had to be topped up with a second power addition. SP is expected to set the briefed 20 to 30 knot overtake in one deliberate movement at the rejoin signal.

error_modes.label: Run in position behind and slightly below No1 clear of wake turbulence

texts.0: SP, due to a run in flown without establishing the aircraft behind and slightly below No1 with a vector towards the low 6 o'clock, did not keep No1 above the horizon during the closure. The aircraft was allowed to climb more than 100 feet through lead level and entered the wake turbulence behind No1, with an uncommanded roll while the closure was still high. The IP took control to displace the aircraft clear of the wake and re-establish the run in geometry.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch attitude that placed No1 on or below the horizon instead of above it, did not fly the run in slightly below lead level as the technique requires. The vertical position reached the 100 foot limit above No1 and the aircraft rode the edge of the prop wash until the IP verbally directed a descent back below lead. The geometry was recovered but only on instruction.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow correction of the vertical reference as the closure developed, did not hold the aircraft clearly below No1 during the run in. The aircraft drifted between 50 and 100 feet high relative to lead level and No1 settled onto the horizon rather than above it. SP identified the shrinking wake clearance, descended back into the low 6 o'clock vector in good time and continued without prompting.
texts.3: SP flew the run in behind and slightly below No1 as briefed, keeping No1 visibly above the horizon and the vertical displacement inside 50 feet of the planned offset throughout the closure. The aircraft stayed clear of the wake turbulence for the whole run in. The vector into the low 6 o'clock was maintained until the bid was made.
texts.4: SP established the run in geometry with negligible error, holding No1 steady above the horizon and the aircraft precisely in the low 6 o'clock vector from the rejoin signal to the bid. Wake clearance was never in question and no vertical correction was needed at any stage. The positional discipline on the run in was exceptional for this point of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP kept the run in within the vertical standards, but the offset below No1 was repeatedly allowed to wash out until lead sat on the horizon before being corrected. The wake clearance remained adequate yet it was recovered rather than protected, and at higher closure rates this will place the aircraft in the prop wash. SP is expected to keep No1 above the horizon continuously through the closure.

error_modes.label: Timing of the bid at the approximately 500 foot range cue

texts.0: SP, due to an inability to read the range from the sight picture, did not make the bid at approximately 500 feet where details on No1 such as the pitot tubes become distinguishable. The bank away from No1 was never started, so the aircraft continued on the closure vector with the overtake still exceeding 15 knots and the range collapsing. The IP intervened on the controls to bank away and prevent an unsafe convergence.
texts.1: SP, due to a range judgement based on the apparent size of the lead aircraft alone, did not begin the bid at the briefed range. The bank away was started well inside 500 feet with the closure still at the 15 knot limit, and it was flown only after the IP called for the bid. The rejoin stayed inside limits but the range cue was not recognized by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the airspeed indicator instead of on the detail available on No1, did not start the bid at the correct range. The bank away was made late, with the overtake still between 5 and 15 knots above the planned value at the bid point. SP saw the pitot tubes come into definition, banked away without prompting and killed the remaining closure in time.
texts.3: SP made the bid at the correct point, banking slightly away from No1 as the range came to approximately 500 feet and the detail on the lead aircraft became distinguishable. The closure at that moment was inside 5 knots of the planned value, so the remaining overtake was manageable with power alone. The range cue of the manual was used as briefed.
texts.4: SP judged the bid point with negligible error, initiating the bank away exactly as the pitot tubes on No1 came into definition and with the closure already trimmed to the planned value. The transition from the run in to the bid was continuous and required no adjustment. Range assessment from the sight picture was of an exceptional standard.
texts.marginal: SP made the bid inside the standards, but on each rejoin it was started slightly late and only after a glance at the airspeed rather than from the detail on No1. The geometry recovered every time, yet the habit of confirming range on the instruments will fail as closure rates increase. SP is expected to take the bid cue from the visual detail on the lead aircraft at approximately 500 feet.

error_modes.label: Bid displacement to two to four ship widths outside No1 wingtip

texts.0: SP, due to a bid flown without a defined aim point, did not bank towards a position two to four ship widths out from No1's wingtip and did not angle the velocity vector away from the lead aircraft. The aircraft arrived with the vector still pointing at No1 and closed inside the wingtip line with the overtake more than 15 knots high. The IP took control to displace the aircraft laterally and stop the convergence.
texts.1: SP, due to a bid made with insufficient bank for the closure being carried, did not achieve the briefed lateral displacement outside No1's wingtip. The aircraft ended up barely one ship width out with the overtake at the 15 knot limit, and the additional bank was applied only after the IP directed it. Lateral spacing was restored but on instruction.
texts.2: SP, due to a bid that was rolled out too early, did not stop the aircraft in the two to four ship width band outside No1's wingtip. The lateral displacement fell short of the briefed band while the closure was still between 5 and 15 knots, so the aim point was not protected. SP recognized the shallow displacement, added bank on his own initiative and re-established the geometry before the route position.
texts.3: SP flew the bid to the correct aim point, arriving two to four ship widths out from No1's wingtip with the velocity vector angling away from the lead aircraft. The residual closure at that point was inside 5 knots of the planned value and could be killed with power alone. The lateral geometry matched the technique of the manual.
texts.4: SP placed the bid with negligible error, rolling into and out of the bank so that the aircraft tracked precisely to the briefed displacement outside No1's wingtip with the vector clearly diverging. No correction to the aim point was needed between the bid and the route position. The lateral control of the rejoin geometry was exceptional for this stage.
texts.marginal: SP achieved a bid displacement inside the standards, but it settled repeatedly at the inner edge of the two to four ship width band and the velocity vector barely diverged from No1. The spacing was legal yet it left no margin if the closure had been higher. SP is expected to bid to a positive displacement with a clearly diverging vector on the following rejoins.

error_modes.label: Killing the overtake with power referenced to No1 line of sight

texts.0: SP, due to a failure to recognize excessive overtake as the range closed, did not reduce the power so that the PCL moved aft in step with No1's aft line of sight in the windscreen. The closure was left unarrested with more than 15 knots of overtake at the route position and the aircraft ran forward of No1. The IP took the throttle and the controls to stop the overshoot developing.
texts.1: SP, due to power being reduced only when the line of sight had already swept well aft, did not match the throttle movement to the rate of the line of sight on No1. The overtake was still at the 15 knot limit as the aircraft arrived abeam and was killed only after the IP called for idle. The rejoin was completed inside limits but the closure was recognized late.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction made in one discrete step rather than tracking the aft movement of No1 in the windscreen, did not kill the overtake progressively. Between 5 and 15 knots of closure remained as the aircraft neared the route position, with a visible aft line of sight rate. SP recognized the excess overtake himself, brought the PCL further aft and stopped the aircraft in position without prompting.
texts.3: SP killed the overtake correctly, moving the PCL aft in proportion to the aft line of sight of No1 in the windscreen so that the closure decayed as the range reduced. The residual overtake at the route position was inside 5 knots and the aircraft stopped without forward travel. The power technique followed the manual as briefed.
texts.4: SP controlled the closure with negligible error, matching the throttle continuously to the line of sight rate on No1 so that the overtake washed out exactly as the route position was reached. No discrete power correction was required and there was no perceptible forward or aft movement on arrival. The energy control was of an exceptional standard for this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP killed the overtake within the standards, but the power reduction always followed the line of sight rather than tracking it, so each arrival needed a late throttle chop. The closure was contained yet the recognition of the overtake was consistently one step behind the sight picture. SP is expected to move the PCL aft in step with No1's aft line of sight rather than in reaction to it.

error_modes.label: Holding separation until closure is controlled before moving to fingertip

texts.0: SP, due to a move towards close position started before the closure rates were under control and the aircraft stabilized in route, did not maintain the lateral and vertical separation required during the deceleration. The aircraft was driven inside the fingertip line while still carrying more than 15 knots of overtake and with the vertical position more than 100 feet off lead level. The IP intervened on the controls to restore separation and stop the closure.
texts.1: SP, due to an early sideways drive towards No1 while the airspeed was still settling, did not hold the separation until stabilized in route. Lateral spacing was reduced with the overtake still at the 15 knot limit and the movement was arrested only after the IP directed a return to route. Separation was regained without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to anticipation of the fingertip position before the route position was consolidated, did not keep the full separation through the last part of the deceleration. The aircraft began closing laterally with between 5 and 15 knots of overtake still present. SP recognized that the closure was not yet controlled, stopped the movement in route and completed the transition to close only once stabilized.
texts.3: SP maintained lateral and vertical separation until the closure rates were under control, stabilizing in route with the overtake inside 5 knots before starting any movement towards close. The transition to fingertip was made as a separate, deliberate step. The sequence of the manual was respected throughout.
texts.4: SP protected the separation with negligible error, arriving in route with the closure already matched and holding the position steady before initiating a smooth, controlled move into fingertip. At no point was spacing traded against an unstabilized closure. The discipline of the rejoin sequence was exceptional for this point of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP held the separation within the standards, but each transition to close was begun while the airspeed was still settling rather than after a clear stabilization in route. The margins were adequate yet the sequence was compressed on every rejoin. SP is expected to stabilize in route with the closure fully controlled before moving into fingertip.

error_modes.label: Straight ahead overshoot on a parallel or divergent vector with idle and speed brake

texts.0: SP, due to an aggressive attempt to save the rejoin instead of accepting the overshoot as soon as the excess overtake was recognized, did not select idle and speed brake and did not maintain lateral spacing on a parallel or divergent vector to No1. The aircraft was flown through the wingtip line with more than 15 knots of closure on a converging vector. The IP took control to establish a divergent vector and dissipate the closure.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed decision to overshoot while the closure was already excessive, did not select idle and the speed brake at the point of recognition. The overtake stayed at the 15 knot limit as the aircraft ran past, and the drag configuration was set only after the IP called for it, although lateral spacing was preserved. The overshoot was safe but IP directed.
texts.2: SP, due to a reluctance to accept that the rejoin could not be saved, did not select idle and speed brake at the first indication of excess overtake. The aircraft went past with between 5 and 15 knots of unarrested closure before the configuration was set. SP made the overshoot decision on his own initiative, held a divergent vector clear of No1 and dissipated the energy without prompting.
texts.3: SP flew the straight ahead overshoot correctly, selecting idle and speed brake as required as soon as the excess overtake was recognized and holding lateral spacing on a parallel or divergent vector to No1. The residual closure was reduced to within 5 knots of matching airspeed before the slide back began. The overshoot followed the technique of the manual.
texts.4: SP recognized the excess overtake immediately and flew an overshoot with negligible error, setting idle and the speed brake without hesitation while tracking a clearly divergent vector away from No1. The closure was dissipated in one controlled action and the geometry never became convergent. The decision making and execution were of an exceptional standard.
texts.marginal: SP flew the overshoot within the standards, but the decision to stop trying to save the rejoin came late on each occasion and the drag configuration followed the decision rather than accompanying it. Spacing was preserved yet the margin shrank every time. SP is expected to make an early overshoot decision and select idle and speed brake as soon as the excess overtake is recognized.

error_modes.label: Speed brake retraction and power increase during the slide back into formation

texts.0: SP, due to the speed brake being left extended and power left at idle while the aircraft slid back into formation, did not increase power prior to achieving matching airspeed with no line of sight on No1. The aircraft decelerated through the route position and fell more than 15 knots below the lead airspeed, ending well aft and out of position. The IP had to advance the power and retract the speed brake to stop the aft movement.
texts.1: SP, due to a late recognition that the line of sight on No1 had stopped, did not retract the speed brake and add power before the airspeeds matched. The aircraft dropped to the 15 knot limit below the lead airspeed and continued aft until the IP called for power and clean configuration. The recovery was completed inside limits but on instruction.
texts.2: SP, due to a power increase timed to the moment the line of sight stopped rather than in anticipation of it, did not prevent an excessive aft movement during the slide back. The airspeed fell between 5 and 15 knots below No1 and the aircraft went further aft than the briefed position. SP identified the developing aft drift, cleaned up the speed brake and added power in good time to regain route without prompting.
texts.3: SP managed the slide back correctly, retracting the speed brake and increasing power before matching airspeed was achieved so that the aircraft stopped in route with no line of sight on No1. The airspeed difference at that moment was inside 5 knots and no aft overshoot developed. The recovery from the overshoot followed the technique of the manual.
texts.4: SP flew the slide back with negligible error, anticipating the matching airspeed so precisely that power and configuration were restored before any aft movement could build. The aircraft settled into route position in a single continuous motion with essentially no airspeed split. The recovery was of an exceptional standard for this stage of training.
texts.marginal: SP recovered from the overshoot within the standards, but power was added only once the line of sight had already stopped, so the aircraft finished slightly aft on each attempt. The result was acceptable yet the aft trend repeated on every overshoot. SP is expected to retract the speed brake and increase power prior to achieving matching airspeed on the following sorties.
